newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top Yeltsin aide pleads against NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Top Yeltsin aide pleads against NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's senior aide on Monday made an impassioned plea against NATO expansion into Eastern Europe, warning it would play into the hands of communists and nationalists.

Anatoly Chubais, chief of staff to the ailing Kremlin leader, also warned that if extension went ahead without a prior binding accord with Russia on security guarantees, Moscow would have to reconsider its overall relationship with the West.

A NATO decision to admit Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic at a key meeting in July "will bring wonderful arguments to the Russian communists and nationalists", he told a news conference at the World Economic Forum.

"It is just what they want. It will make them much stronger," declared Chubais -- better known from earlier appearances at the annual gathering of global business and political leaders as a proponent of economic reform.

His remarks, billed in advance in Moscow as a major statement, closely followed similar warnings issued at the Forum last week by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, deputy foreign minister Alexander Avdeyev and first deputy chairman of parliament, Alexander Shokhin.

The decision to send Chubais to reinforce their pleas appeared to have been taken in the hope of using his popularity with U.S. and European businessmen who attend the Forum to convince them to intervene with their governments.

After arriving in the Swiss mountain resort on Sunday, he has had private meetings with his old Forum contacts, including international financier George Soros, clearly to reinforce the warning before giving the news conference.

Chubais, who in the first half of the 1990s was in charge of the Russian privatisation programme, said Moscow wanted a "binding agreement" giving guarantees that NATO troops and nuclear weapons would not be moved close to Russia's borders.

If such an accord were concluded and signed before the expansion -- which would only go into effect in 1999 -- was formally approved, it would help alleviate the effect on Russian public opinion, he said.

But if it went ahead without that, "it would be the worst political mistake made by the West for 50 years," Chubais declared amid sceptical questioning from journalists and officials from former Soviet bloc states in the hall.
"Such a decision would change the whole political landscape in Russia, and would inevitably lead to a rethinking of foreign policy," he said.

This would include reconsideration of Russia's relationship with the International Monetary Fund, its membership of the Strasbourg-based Council of Europe, and its application to join the Geneva-based World Trade Organisation.

Chubais said ordinary Russians were presently more concerned with the economy and living standards, but as time went by could be swayed by the arguments of anti-Western figures like Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky.

He made no mention of former Yeltsin adviser Alexander Lebed, but Western experts on Russia in Davos say they believe the Kremlin is most concerned that the ex-army general might use the NATO issue to build on his already wide popularity.

Lebed, who had sought an invitation to attend the Forum but was refused, has called for the ailing Yeltsin to stand down and declared he will run for the presidency in new elections. Current opinion polls suggest he could win easily.

Yeltsin himself raised the NATO expansion issue in talks on Sunday with President Jacques Chirac of France. Chirac said afterwards he thought an agreement providing guarantees could be reached before the alliance's July summit in Madrid.
